claims.text: Cold-spray deposition of a reinforced metal composite can produce a dense repair layer.
The cold-sprayed repair layer will be nanostructured.
Cold-spray repair will minimize hot-cracking risk relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
Cold-spray repair will improve surface hardness relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
Cold-spray repair will improve wear resistance relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
Cold-spray repair will improve corrosion resistance in aggressive environments relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The damaged annealed alloy surface is prone to hot cracking when subjected to high heat input.
The initial surface contains microstructural defects and has relatively low surface hardness.
Keeping the process below the material's recrystallization threshold will prevent thermally induced defects.
Cold spraying can create a well-adhered layer with minimal porosity.
High-velocity particle impact during cold spraying induces grain refinement.
The refined, low-porosity repair layer increases load-bearing capacity and distributes stresses more uniformly.
High-velocity particle impact produces a strong mechanical bond between deposited material and the substrate.
Solid-state cold-spray deposition avoids the high thermal gradients and residual stresses that cause hot cracking during fusion welding.
Ceramic reinforcement introduces a hard, wear-resistant phase into the repair layer.
Cold-spray repair will significantly reduce surface-crack initiation relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
Traditional fusion-welded repairs are prone to hot cracking and inconsistent microstructures.
Untreated surfaces have lower hardness and durability under aggressive service conditions.
The benefits of cold-spray repair depend on optimization of coating density, adhesion, alloy formulation, and spraying parameters.
The repair benefits may be lost if service conditions exceed the thermal or mechanical limits of the deposited layer.
